enrichment.short_title: Knostrop sewage works SBR performance dispute
key_facts: Yorkshire Water engaged Taylor Woodrow under an IChemE Red Book design-and-build contract to upgrade the Knostrop sewage treatment works serving Leeds.
The dispute centred on a sequencing batch reactor (SBR) supplied and installed by Taylor Woodrow, with Biwater as process sub-contractor.
Yorkshire Water alleged the SBR could not meet contractual capacity and effluent quality requirements, citing solids carry-over, selector capacity and nitrification failures.
Extensive expert evidence addressed sludge age, SSVI, microthrix parvicella control, industrial pollution in influent and Phase 1 remedial works.

Treatment and selector capacity, solids carry-over and nitrification

notes: CGT qualifying loan appeal on case stated; s.253 TCGA 1992 analysis and Edwards v Bairstow review are clear.

enrichment.short_title: CGT relief refused on non-qualifying refinance loan
key_facts: Mr Robson appealed by case stated against an estimated CGT assessment on the 1994-95 disposal of High Yedmandale Farm for a gain of about £148,950.
He claimed s.253(4) relief after paying £151,000 from the sale proceeds to Barclays in reduction of a company term loan he had guaranteed.
The General Commissioners found the 1993 refinance loan was not a qualifying loan because prior borrowing had funded work on Mr Robson's Queen Street property rather than the company's trade.
Records were poor, with no invoices or contracts for substantial company work done for the controlling shareholder.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court appeal by way of case stated from the General Commissioners on TCGA 1992 s.253.
enrichment.outcome: Taxpayer's appeal dismissed; the 1993 loan was not a qualifying loan and, although the Commissioners could accept the guarantee payment point, that issue did not arise once the loan failed s.253(1).
enrichment.ratio: Under s.253(1) TCGA 1992 the inquiry is to the use made of the loan; a refinance loan does not become qualifying merely by consolidating existing borrowing unless the replaced indebtedness was itself used wholly to serve the borrower's trade, and refinancing non-qualifying personal borrowing on improved terms does not convert it into a qualifying loan.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'qualifying loan' in s.253(1) TCGA 1992
Whether a refinance loan must be judged by the use of the replaced borrowing
Whether s.253(4) guarantee relief was available on the facts found
Appropriateness of Edwards v Bairstow review of General Commissioners' findings
linked_authorities: Morgan v Tate & Lyle Ltd [1955] AC 21
Strong & Co of Romsey Ltd v Woodifield [1906] AC 448
Bentleys, Stokes & Lowless v Beeson (HMIT) [1952] 33 TC 491
Vodafone Cellular Ltd v Shaw (HMIT) [1997] STC 734

confidence.notes: Outcome, statutory reasoning and key facts are explicit throughout the case stated appeal.

notes: Unfair prejudice petition on secret property acquisition; buy-out relief in principle though form of order deferred.

enrichment.short_title: Unfair prejudice over secret landlord property purchase
key_facts: Baumler (UK) Limited was an equal two-director company importing Hans Baumler clothing, with Mr Gerrard holding 490 shares and Mr Koby 510 shares.
The company operated from Geko House under leases from landlord Sarena Limited and had opportunities from 1999 to buy the surrounding Property.
Mr Koby secretly procured purchase of the Property by Howard Ronson's Vermeer Properties for £1.35m, excluding Mr Gerrard and the company from the transaction.
Relations broke down and Mr Gerrard petitioned for unfair prejudice, seeking a buy-out order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 461 unfair prejudice petition in the Companies Court.
enrichment.outcome: Petition succeeded in principle; Mr Gerrard's interests were unfairly prejudiced and relief should include a buy-out order, with the precise form of buy-out left for further argument.
enrichment.ratio: Where a quasi-partnership company required unanimity on major decisions, a majority director's secret arrangement for an associate to acquire property the company was seeking to buy, for his own benefit and contrary to the relationship of mutual confidence, amounted to unfair prejudice warranting buy-out relief.
legal_issues: Whether Mr Koby's conduct amounted to unfair prejudice under section 461
Whether secret procurement of the Property purchase breached fiduciary duties and quasi-partnership expectations
What buy-out order was appropriate between minority and majority shareholders

confidence.notes: Findings of unfair prejudice and provisional buy-out relief are clear; only the final form of the buy-out order was deferred.

notes: Theft appeal; inadequate good character direction quashed conviction; no retrial in public interest. Judges metadata lists historical Law Lords.

enrichment.short_title: Theft conviction quashed for inadequate good character direction
key_facts: Bailey removed nickel belonging to Western Mining Corporation after a shortfall in metal owed to him by AMA.
He sold the nickel despite police advice that it belonged to Western Mining; the jury had to decide dishonesty.
The Recorder gave a brief good character direction near the end of a two-day summing-up without linking character to propensity to dishonesty.
CPS accepted a retrial was not in the public interest after the community order was served and compensation was settled via insurers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal after Gage J refused leave; renewed permission granted.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction quashed; no retrial ordered; defendants costs order made for permission application costs.
enrichment.ratio: Where dishonesty is the central issue, a good character direction must adequately explain how absence of previous convictions bears on the defendant's propensity to act dishonestly; an inadequate direction renders the conviction unsafe.
legal_issues: Adequacy of good character direction in a dishonesty theft trial
Whether conviction is unsafe without a retrial
Defendants costs order for privately funded permission application

confidence.notes: Outcome and direction defect are clear; judges metadata corrupted.

notes: Permission to appeal on samosa production line warranties, implied fitness and damages; costs stay conditions are clear.

enrichment.short_title: Permission to appeal on samosa pastry line warranties
area_of_law: Sale of goods and supply of services

statutes_considered.title: Supply of Goods and Services Act 1982

key_facts: Filobake bought a divided production line from Rondo and Frampton to extrude, bake and cool filo pastry for commercial samosa production.
Each supplier gave performance warranties, but HHJ Seymour QC construed the first defendant's warranty narrowly and did not fully analyse implied fitness for purpose or damages.
Expert evidence showed the line could not produce pastry with sufficient longitudinal strength or target moisture for acceptable samosas.
Filobake had failed to pay a £30,000 costs-on-account order while seeking permission to appeal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Single Lord Justice permission to appeal application after trial on breach and quantum.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted generally; further £30,000 costs-on-account payment stayed unless second defendant's solicitors undertake to repay it if the appeal succeeds.
enrichment.ratio: It is arguable that performance warranties requiring production of samosa pastry to an attached recipe, together with implied fitness-for-purpose obligations on divided equipment, were construed too narrowly and that damages for lost profits or wasted expenditure warrant review if breach is established.
legal_issues: Construction of express performance warranties for samosa pastry production
Implied fitness for purpose where equipment from two suppliers was intended to operate together
Allocation of risk where moisture content assumptions differed between suppliers
Whether damages for lost profits or wasted expenditure were wrongly rejected

confidence.notes: Permission reasoning and interim costs order are explicit, though full trial findings were not reviewed on the merits.

notes: Arbitration Act 1996 challenge to interest award; jurisdiction and issue estoppel analysis is detailed and outcome clear.

enrichment.short_title: Partial set-aside of arbitrator's pre-1995 interest award
key_facts: Westland retained Saudi lawyer Al-Hejailan under a 1985 engagement letter with a success fee for settling claims against Saudi Arabia over the Arab Organisation for Industrialisation dispute.

After Kerr J's interim award rejected a success fee but reserved quantum meruit on hourly rates, Tackaberry QC valued work by a notional annual retainer of US $450,000 and awarded substantial interest.
Westland challenged interest under sections 67 and 68, having not earlier challenged jurisdiction over the retainer methodology for commercial reasons.
Interest had been expressly abandoned before Kerr but partially revived in a 2001 letter and at the 2001 hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court applications under sections 67 and 68 of the Arbitration Act 1996 to set aside parts of a second interim arbitral award.
enrichment.outcome: Interest for the period before January 1995 was set aside for want of jurisdiction; interest from 1995 was within jurisdiction and not affected by serious irregularity under section 68.
enrichment.ratio: Where a claimant withdraws an interest claim from the reference it may be reinstated only if clearly revived and not objected to; an arbitrator could award interest from 1995 but not for an earlier period never referred, and Westland was estopped from challenging the capital award methodology it had failed to challenge within section 70(3).
legal_issues: Whether the arbitrator had jurisdiction to award interest after an earlier abandonment
Whether issue estoppel prevented challenging the retainer-based capital award when attacking interest
Whether failure to allow submissions amounted to serious irregularity under section 68
Scope of section 73 where jurisdiction could have been raised at the 2001 hearing
linked_authorities: Fidelitas Shipping Ltd v V/o Exportchleb [1966] QB 630
JSC Zestafoni G Nikoladze Ferroalloy Plant v Ronly Holdings Ltd [2004] EWHC 245 (Comm)
Westland Helicopters Ltd v Arab Organisation for Industrialisation [1994] 2 Lloyd's Rep 608

confidence.notes: Detailed reasoning on jurisdiction, estoppel and section 68 is explicit with a clear split outcome on interest periods.

notes: Race Relations Act s.11 organisation classification appeal; MPS held to be an organisation of workers.

enrichment.short_title: Medical defence society is organisation of workers under RRA

statutes_considered.title: Trade Union and Labour Relations (Consolidation) Act 1992

key_facts: Dr Sadek, an NHS doctor and MPS member, claimed race discrimination after the Medical Protection Society stopped funding employment tribunal advice.
The employment tribunal and EAT held the MPS was an organisation within section 11(1), giving the tribunal jurisdiction.
The MPS is a mutual medical defence organisation providing advice, representation and indemnities to medical and allied professionals.
The Court of Appeal had to decide whether the MPS was an 'organisation of workers' and/or an 'other organisation' whose members carry on a profession.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on a preliminary jurisdiction issue in an employment tribunal race discrimination claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the MPS is an organisation of workers within section 11(1) so the employment tribunal had jurisdiction.
enrichment.ratio: Profession is widely defined in the Race Relations Act and medical practitioners may be workers; the MPS, whose members practise professions and receive membership benefits, falls within the first category of section 11(1), and the third 'any other organisation' category is unavailable where the first category applies.
legal_issues: Whether the MPS is an 'organisation of workers' under section 11(1) RRA 1976
Relationship between the first and third categories in section 11(1)
Whether professional/client exclusions in other employment statutes apply
Whether alternative remedies under section 25 in the county court were sufficient

confidence.notes: Statutory construction, facts about the MPS and appeal outcome are clearly stated.

notes: Slip rule permission appeal with immediate disposal; remittal for quantum rehearing is clearly ordered.

enrichment.short_title: Slip rule correction set aside and damages remitted
key_facts: Mr Heather sued Mr Greenacre and Mr Griffiths over a 1994 agreement to employ him in Nene Packaging Ltd and grant him 30% of the shares.
After settlement with Greenacre for £15,000, Griffiths was absent at the liability trial and judgment for damages to be assessed followed.
HHJ Metcalf awarded £6,758 for lost salary but no share loss, then corrected the order to nil under the slip rule after omitting the £15,000 settlement credit.
Both litigants acted in person and disputed whether the later correction was a permissible slip correction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Single Lord Justice permission to appeal application treated as an immediate appeal on CPR 40.12 slip rule correction.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; appeals allowed; orders of 2 and 9 October 2003 set aside and the case remitted to Northampton County Court to determine whether total damages exceed £15,000.
enrichment.ratio: Where a judge plainly failed to deduct an agreed settlement payment from assessed damages, it is arguable whether post-sealing correction under CPR 40.12 was within power; on appeal the proper course was to set aside both orders and remit quantum rather than leave conflicting orders in place.
legal_issues: Scope of CPR 40.12 slip rule after an order has been sealed and issued
Whether correction of a major deduction was a slip or a change of mind
Appropriate disposal where both parties sought permission to appeal
Assessment of loss of salary and share value in a packaging business venture
linked_authorities: Bristol-Myers Squibb Company v Baker Norton Pharmaceuticals Inc [2001] EWCA Civ 414

confidence.notes: Procedural history, slip rule issue and remittal order are all explicit.

notes: CITES condemnation JR on CEMA s.141 ejusdem generis and proportionality; scope narrowed to 39 birds.

enrichment.short_title: Endangered parrot condemnation upheld under section 141 CEMA

statutes_considered.title: Control of Trade in Endangered Species (Enforcement) Regulations 1997

key_facts: Customs seized 144 endangered parrots from Mr Sissen's Cornhill Conservation Centre after convictions for smuggling Lear's and Blue-Headed Macaws.
A magistrate would have returned 100 birds, but the Crown Court condemned more; on review the challenge was narrowed to 39 birds of specified species.
The Crown Court found Mr Sissen was a serial smuggler who kept poor records, mixed flocks and could conceal illegally imported birds among lawfully bred stock.
Mr Sissen argued section 141 required species-by-species linkage and that birds in separate aviaries were not 'found with' unlawfully imported birds.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of Crown Court condemnation proceedings that should have proceeded by case stated.
enrichment.outcome: Judicial review dismissed; condemnation of the 39 birds upheld, with proportionality balancing personal mitigation against enforcement of CITES obligations; Customs costs reduced to £13,000.
enrichment.ratio: Section 141(1)(b) CEMA applies disjunctively and, in enforcing CITES trade controls, endangered birds of like kind kept on the same premises may be treated as found with unlawfully imported specimens without requiring identical species or common aviaries; proportionality did not favour return given repeated offending and deliberate concealment.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'mixed, packed or found' in section 141(1)(b) CEMA
Whether ejusdem generis requires species-specific matching of seized birds
Reverse burden of proof under section 154 and Regulation 5
Whether condemnation was disproportionate given prior sentence and confiscation
linked_authorities: R v Uxbridge Justices ex parte Webb [1993] 162 JP 198
Travell v Commissioners of Customs and Excise [1997] 162 JP 181
Lindsay v Customs and Excise Commissioners [2002] 1 WLR 1766
Customs and Excise Commissioners v Air Canada [1991] 2 QB 446

confidence.notes: Grounds, factual findings, narrowed bird count and outcome are clear despite an opaque Crown Court judgment.

notes: Permission to appeal refused on liquidator misfeasance findings; Park J's insolvency and fiduciary duty analysis treated as unassailable.

enrichment.short_title: Permission refused on director misfeasance over sale proceeds
key_facts: The liquidator of MDA Investment Management Ltd challenged Mr Doney for misfeasance and breach of fiduciary duty over a July 1998 business sale.
About £1 million cash went to the company but over half the £2.4 million total consideration was diverted to the MDA partnership in which Mr Doney was the largest partner.
Park J found the company was cash-flow insolvent and Mr Doney had diverted sale value to himself while creditors remained unpaid.
Mr Doney also failed to obtain relief under section 727 and the judge refused to exercise discretion in his favour.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against Park J's trial and supplementary judgments.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused with costs assessed at £5,000.
enrichment.ratio: Where a trial judge has made detailed findings that an insolvent company's director diverted more than half the proceeds of a business sale to a partnership he controlled, an appellate court will not interfere with misfeasance and breach of fiduciary duty conclusions or the refusal of section 727 relief on a mere disagreement with fact-finding.
legal_issues: Whether misfeasance required proof of balance sheet insolvency or only cash-flow insolvency
Whether diverted sale proceeds were surplus rather than creditor property
Correct approach to section 727 relief from liability for misfeasance
Whether Park J's exercise of discretion on section 727 was open to appeal

confidence.notes: Permission refusal reasoning and core findings relied on are clearly summarised, though the full trial judgment is not reproduced.
